items.title: Putin Breaks Down His Isolation, With a Big Assist From Trump
items.summary: Notching wins from Washington, the Russian leader is talking with foreign leaders and could return to diplomatic center stage with possible summit meetings.
items.full_text:
Title: Putin Breaks Down His Isolation, With a Big Assist From Trump - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/world/europe/putin-isolation-breakdown-trump.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:31:24 GMT

Markdown Content:
He took a [rare call](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/world/europe/norway-finland-putin-call.html) from the Finnish and Norwegian leaders. He hosted Qatar’s emir and Iran’s president at a forum of gas-exporting countries.

And he squired African heads of state around a Moscow exhibition, advising them to control social media networks in their own nations, or risk [mass protests like those that have gripped France](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/europe/france-protests-timeline.html). There, he promoted Russia’s answer to Starlink, but said Russia was in close contact with Elon Musk, whom he called “a brilliant man.”

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia engaged in a frenzy of diplomatic activity in the Russian capital this past week that underscored how, nearly five years into his war against Ukraine, he is thwarting Western attempts to isolate him and muscling his way back to center stage in global affairs.

Mr. Putin has been winning praise, high-level meeting invitations and concessions from the United States, even while escalating the war and showing no intention of compromising. The news that the Trump administration is [considering lifting sanctions](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/us/politics/russia-fund-sanctions-trump.html) on Russia’s flagship government investment fund came after President Trump [agreed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/us/politics/trump-russia-diesel-putin.html) to import Russian diesel fuel and the U.S. special envoy, Steve Witkoff, [praised](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/russia-american-prisoner-release-stephen-hubbard-trump.html) Mr. Putin as a humanitarian.

“In the Kremlin, I think they are really celebrating,” said Stefan Meister, a Russia analyst at the German Council on Foreign Relations. He added, “No matter what they are doing or not doing, they are getting things they didn’t even expect.”

Mr. Putin is slated to travel to Shenzhen, China, in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, where a possible trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and Mr. Trump would put Russia on apparently equal footing with the two global superpowers. He could then go to Miami in December for the Group of 20 summit, should he accept an invitation that Mr. Trump extended, to the dismay of some U.S. allies.

As Mr. Putin chips away at his ostracism in the West, relations between the United States and Ukraine have continued to deteriorate, underscoring [Kyiv’s vulnerability](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/world/europe/ukraine-starlink-energy.html) ahead of what is expected to be the worst winter of the war.

Image

The scene in Kherson, Ukraine, where the streets are covered in netting to protect against drone attacks. Credit...David Guttenfelder/The New York Times

Last month, Mr. Trump publicly [urged](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/11/world/europe/trump-zelensky-diesel-energy-russia-.html) Ukrainians to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky and called him an obstacle to peace. Then the Ukrainian military [lost some critical access](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/world/europe/starshield-starlink-ukraine.html) to the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet constellation. Ukraine is [running low on U.S.-made air defenses](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/06/world/europe/ukraine-russia-missile-defense-patriots.html).

For years, Mr. Putin has suggested that he can outlast the resolve of Ukraine’s American and European backers. With Mr. Trump turning against Kyiv and [entertaining more deals with Moscow,](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/us/trump-putin-russia-sanctions.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share) while unrest and a [potential debt crisis](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/business/france-bond-yields.html)[boost](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/world/europe/france-unrest-political-center.html) the far right in France, Mr. Putin may feel that his waiting is about to pay off.

“Putin has the impression that he was right,” Mr. Meister said. “That he had to wait it out and in the end he can get more than he could have dreamed of from Trump.”

As the rift between the United States and Ukraine grows, Europe has reached a perilous moment, struggling to agree on whether to speak directly to Mr. Putin and if so, who should do the talking.

President Alexander Stubb of Finland and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store of Norway called Mr. Putin on Tuesday, in what Mr. Putin later characterized as a sign that some European leaders want constructive dialogue.

The call prompted controversy within Europe, with Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark accusing the Finnish and Norwegian leaders of “going solo.”

But Mr. Meister said the call was a recognition of the danger facing Europe. “They are really afraid there is a breaking point and we are losing the U.S.,” he said.

For weeks, Mr. Putin has been criticizing European leaders, accusing them of taking on too much debt, driving up costs for their people by refusing Russian gas, and failing to represent their society’s real interests by sending aid to Ukraine.

Image

An image of Mr. Putin in Moscow last month.Credit...Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters

“Europe is dealing a blow to its own industry and social sector by abandoning Russian energy supplies and tearing up long-term contracts,” he said at a gas exporters’ event in Moscow on Tuesday. “You know, there is a saying in Russian: ‘Don’t dig a pit for others, or you may fall into it yourself.’”

Hanna Notte, an analyst at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and the author of a book on Mr. Putin’s foreign policy, “We Shall Outlast Them,” said the Russian leader was clearly aiming his comments at France and Germany, where far-right parties are popular and campaigning on ending support for Ukraine. The French far-right leader, Marine Le Pen, leads in polling for the presidential election next spring.

“This is the line that Russia has been pushing for a while, and it makes total sense to do this ahead of elections in various European countries,” Ms. Notte said.

The aim, Ms. Notte said, is to convince European voters that politicians “are not acting in the interests of their own people, that they are spending all that money to militarize, to prepare for a war against Russia, instead of dealing with their own social problems at home — exhibit A being France and the protests.”

items.title: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
items.summary: After losing ground in Israel’s election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu must draw on decades of political capital and reckon with old foes if he is to build a governing coalition.
items.full_text:
Title: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/world/middleeast/netanyahu-coalition-building-tests-political-skills.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:30:27 GMT

Markdown Content:
For Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, putting together a new governing coalition after Israel’s inconclusive election would be like assembling a jigsaw puzzle with ill-fitting pieces.

Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving leader, [lost ground](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/world/middleeast/israel-election-results-netanyahu-eisenkot.html), with his Likud party failing to hold nearly a sixth of its seats in the Parliament, and his hawkish coalition seeing its share decline even more. But to the surprise of some political observers, Likud still emerged as the largest party with 27 seats.

If Mr. Netanyahu manages to get the green light from Israel’s president to try to form a government — not a given at this point — he will need 61 seats to retain power.

To do so, he must find a way to expand his coalition of far-right nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, perhaps by luring at least eight defectors from an opposition bloc that has vowed to unseat him. Or he could try to create a national unity government with Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former military chief who heads the center-right Yashar, the largest party in the anti-Netanyahu alliance.

To achieve either goal, Mr. Netanyahu, 77, would have to draw on decades of parliamentary savvy and political capital. He would also have to overcome a legacy of grievances he has left over a career of political skirmishes and, critics say, betrayals.

## From Division to Unity?

The prime minister’s bloc now controls five more seats than the main opposition bloc, a politically diverse alliance of Jewish parties led by Mr. Eisenkot. But if Mr. Eisenkot were to partner with two predominantly Arab parties, who also oppose Mr. Netanyahu, the coalition would muster a comfortable majority of 67 seats to take power.

Some Jewish parties in the opposition have so far ruled that out, but Mr. Eisenkot could still be the one with the first chance of forming a government.

Mr. Eisenkot has in the past cooperated with Mr. Netanyahu, in the days after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, [joining his emergency war cabinet](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/14/world/middleeast/israel-war-cabinet-gaza-netanyahu.html) to help steer the conflict in Gaza. Mr. Eisenkot’s political partner at the time, Benny Gantz, another former military chief and opponent of Mr. Netanyahu, joined the war cabinet as well.

They both [left the government](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/09/world/middleeast/gantz-quits-israel-netanyahu.html) eight months later, frustrated with what they said was Mr. Netanyahu’s failure to design an exit strategy for the war and a diplomatic plan for Gaza’s future.

Image

A Likud party campaign ad featuring Mr. Netanyahu and President Trump last week in Jerusalem.Credit...Ohad Zwigenberg/Associated Press

Mr. Netanyahu did not take any responsibility for Israel’s failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attack, instead blaming his generals. Mr. Eisenkot, who lost a son in the fighting in Gaza, declared Mr. Netanyahu unworthy of remaining in office and founded Yashar to unseat the prime minister.

In earlier years, Mr. Netanyahu had adopted a different strategy, trying to bring centrist parties into his coalitions.

“It was a mechanism that allowed him to shift the blame if he made moderate decisions that were unpopular with his constituency,” said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group.

Many Israelis would like to see a unity government. Forming one with Mr. Eisenkot’s party and possibly others in the opposition could require Mr. Netanyahu to abandon his most contentious policies, such as his government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary.

Mr. Netanyahu formed his hawkish government four years ago when mainstream parties refused to sit in a coalition with him after he was indicted in 2019 on charges of corruption, which he has denied.

Some critics say that Mr. Netanyahu has moved too far to the right to see a way back. “Netanyahu is a secular, liberal democrat. At least he was originally,” Ben Caspit, a political commentator and biographer of Mr. Netanyahu, wrote on Thursday in Maariv, a Hebrew newspaper. He noted that the prime minister had “displayed ideological flexibility and pragmatism countless times in the past.”

“Might he in his old age be capable of re-embracing the values he was raised on?” he asked. “I don’t know and I find it hard to believe that is possible.”

Image

Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Mr. Netanyahu’s main challenger, in September. His coalition fell short of an outright majority in the election.Credit...Amit Elkayam for The New York Times

## A Question of Trust

Previous efforts by Mr. Netanyahu to work with centrists have not ended well for them.

In 2014, Mr. Netanyahu [fired](https://www.nytimes.com/2014/12/03/world/middleeast/israel-netanyahu-cabinet-elections.html) his centrist finance and justice ministers, then engineered the dissolution of Parliament and brought about early elections.

In 2020, Mr. Gantz, a centrist, entered a unity government in a power-sharing arrangement with Mr. Netanyahu to help battle the coronavirus pandemic. That government collapsed seven months later, after Mr. Netanyahu [violated agreements](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/22/world/middleeast/israel-election-netanyahu.html) he had made with Mr. Gantz as a condition for him joining the government.

Mr. Gantz and his party have since lost so much support that he dropped out of this election race shortly before the vote.

“I don’t know if Netanyahu can convince anyone to join him now because it’s political suicide,” said Gadi Wolfsfeld, a professor of political communication at Reichman University in Herzliya.

## Shaky Histories

If Mr. Netanyahu is looking to pick off defectors from Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc, two right-leaning parties, Together and Yisrael Beitenu, would both seem good ideological fits.

But their respective leaders, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, are former associates turned bitter foes, and their relationships with the prime minister have deteriorated.

Image

Netanyahu supporters, in the back, are separated by the police as they argued last week with left-wing activists calling for a government with Arab parties.Credit...David Goldman/Associated Press

Mr. Bennett worked as chief of staff to Mr. Netanyahu two decades ago, when the Likud leader was in the opposition. Mr. Liberman helped shepherd Mr. Netanyahu to his first victory in 1996 and became the director-general of the prime minister’s office.

Mr. Liberman had an [ugly breakup with Mr. Netanyahu](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/16/world/middleeast/netanyahu-liberman-israel-election.html) over a personal slight in the late 1990s and left Likud to set up his own party.

Mr. Liberman subsequently joined Netanyahu-led coalitions, but he quit or was fired from five governments. Mr. Liberman brought down the government in 2018, complaining of a soft policy toward Hamas, then refused to cooperate with Mr. Netanyahu after a string of inconclusive elections.

Positioning himself as a secularist, Mr. Liberman has vowed not to join coalitions that include Mr. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox allies, or what Mr. Liberman calls “messianists.”

The day before the election, Mr. Liberman called on the attorney general to investigate Mr. Netanyahu on suspicion of treason, accusing him of trying to set off a new military confrontation with Iran to delay the elections.

Mr. Bennett became prime minister in 2021 at the head of a short-lived, anti-Netanyahu government that included parties across the political spectrum, including a conservative Arab Islamic party.

Mr. Netanyahu publicly expressed his low opinion of Mr. Bennett in a 2023 autobiography, “Bibi: My Story.” “Though he postured as right-wing, I gradually understood that this was an empty pose. He craved fame and power,” Mr. Netanyahu wrote of Mr. Bennett.

Image

Naftali Bennett, a former Israeli prime minister, at a campaign event last month in Jerusalem.Credit...Ohad Zwigenberg/Associated Press

If Mr. Netanyahu is unable to build a governing coalition, political analysts say he is banking on nobody else being able to do so either. And in the meantime, Mr. Netanyahu remains the head of a caretaker government and may prefer to wait for another election.

“That would be a relatively good outcome for Netanyahu,” Mr. Plesner said. The opposition might have a harder time mobilizing supporters a second time around, he said, adding, “another election might be an opportunity for Netanyahu to improve his showing.”

items.title: Where Do Israel’s Arab Parties Stand?
items.summary: Having won a record 19 seats in Israel’s Parliament, the two Arab-led parties say they want to work with opposition factions to take down the Netanyahu government.
items.full_text:
Title: Where Do Israel’s Arab Parties Stand? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/world/middleeast/israel-arab-parties.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:32:09 GMT

Markdown Content:
One of the biggest surprises of the Israeli elections was the success of the two Arab-led political parties, Raam and the Joint List. They collectively won 19 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament.

Raam is an Islamist party and the Joint List is an alliance of three factions that includes leftists and Palestinian nationalists.

Raam has sought to gain acceptance from other opposition parties in Israel by putting less emphasis on the plight of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza and focusing more on issues plaguing Arab citizens of Israel, like violent crime and discriminatory housing policies.

While the Joint List has also fought for the rights of Arab citizens of Israel, it frequently criticizes Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and has called itself “a genuine democratic alternative to the racist Zionist consensus.”

The outcome of the voting [excited many Arab voters](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/30/world/middleeast/arab-voters-israel-election-taibe.html), and both parties have said they are willing to work with the Israeli opposition in taking down Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. But many members of the Jewish-led opposition have ruled out cooperating with the Arab parties to form a new government, and strongly object to a number of their views. Many Israelis fear Arab parties wielding influence over foreign affairs and security issues, and disagree on how to address the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Here is a look at the positions of the Joint List — an alliance of the Hadash, Balad and Taal parties — and Raam.

## Hadash

Image

Yousef Jabareen, the leader of Israel’s Arab-led Joint List in the Arab-Israeli town of Umm al-Fahm, on Wednesday.Credit...Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Hadash is a leftist Arab-Jewish faction whose name is an acronym that stands for the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality.

The party’s [website](https://hadash.org.il/#values) says it supports Israel withdrawing from the West Bank, Gaza and the Golan Heights, returning Israel to its pre-1967 border and recognizing “the right of the Arab Palestinian people to its self-determination and establishing its independent state.”

It also calls for resolving the Palestinian refugee issue in accordance with United Nations resolutions. U.N. General Assembly resolution 194 calls for allowing Palestinian refugees to return to their homes, while offering compensation to those who elect not to return for lost or damaged property.

Unlike other members of the Joint List, one of Hadash’s elected representatives is Jewish.

Hadash, founded in 1977, also supports “total equality for Arab citizens”; reducing military expenditures; ending funding for settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank; recognizing Arab citizens of Israel as “a national minority on the political, social and cultural levels”; passing legislation to reinforce the equality of women; and banning weapons of mass destruction, according to the party’s website.

Party leaders have criticized the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Ayman Odeh, who was the chairman of Hadash until May, referred to “Hamas’s murderous attack” in an [opinion article](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/10/19/opinion/israel-netanyahu-palestinians.html) for The New York Times.

His successor is Yousef Jabareen, a human rights lawyer who studied law at Georgetown University in Washington.

On Friday, he said in an interview that the Joint List was hoping to work with other opposition parties to remove Mr. Netanyahu from office.

“The years of Netanyahu, Ben Gvir and Smotrich have been awful,” he said, referring to two far-right government ministers. “So our top priority is to get rid of their government.”

## Balad

Image

Balad’s chairman, Sami Abu Shehadeh, in October in Tel Aviv.Credit...Ammar Awad/Reuters

Balad is a Palestinian nationalist party whose name is an acronym for the National Democratic Assembly. The party, founded in the mid-1990s, has emphasized that Israel should become “a state for all of its citizens” — a position that is anathema to many Israelis, who say that it seeks to undermine Israel’s Jewish character.

Many of Balad’s positions are similar to those of Hadash. It also wants Israel to withdraw to its pre-1967 borders and to recognize Arab citizens as a national minority.

Balad officials have said they want Arab citizens to have autonomy over their educational system, including the ability to develop their own curriculums.

Lawmakers from Balad have sometimes found themselves entangled with the Israeli authorities. In 2007, Azmi Bishara, a founder of the party, was accused by the Israeli authorities of spying for Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group. He has denied wrongdoing and has since relocated to Qatar, where he serves as director general of the Arab Institute for Policy and Research Studies.

Haneen Zoabi, another former Balad member of Parliament, was temporarily blocked from participating in Knesset discussions in 2011 after being on board a [Turkish flotilla raided by Israeli commandos](http://www.nytimes.com/2010/06/01/world/middleeast/01flotilla.html) as it tried to breach the naval blockade of Gaza. And Sami Abu Shahadeh, the current chairman of Balad, faced scrutiny after he wrote an article describing the Oct. 7 attack as “an important historic event in the military sense.”

He later condemned the attack, after the Israeli Supreme Court discussed disqualifying him from running for Parliament. At the urging of the court, he withdrew from Balad’s slate of candidates in this election.

## Taal

Image

Ahmad Tibi last week in the Arab village of Taibe, in northern Israel.Credit...Ammar Awad/Reuters

Taal is an Arab party led by Ahmad Tibi, who has served in the Knesset for more than 25 years. The party’s name is an acronym that means the Arab Movement for Change.

Mr. Tibi, who founded Taal in the mid-1990s, has long expressed support for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and an Israeli withdrawal to pre-1967 borders. Like other Arab parties, he has also advocated solutions to rampant crime in Arab communities in Israel.

In the 1990s, he served as an adviser to Yasir Arafat, the leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization.

After joining the Knesset in 1999, Mr. Tibi told The Times about the complexity of pledging allegiance to Israel. “I can live with it,” he said. “I didn’t pledge allegiance to the Zionism of the state, but to the State of Israel that I would like to be mine, as a citizen.”

In the aftermath of the Oct. 7 attacks, he said Arab citizens were opposed to targeting civilians.

On Wednesday, he said the Joint List was “ready to swallow frogs to take down Netanyahu’s government.”

## Raam

Image

Mansour Abbas, the head of the Raam party, in October in Nazareth.Credit...Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Raam is a socially conservative Islamist party whose name is an acronym for the United Arab List. [Mansour Abbas](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/world/middleeast/israel-mansour-abbas.html) leads the party and has spearheaded its efforts to play a more influential role in Israeli politics.

In 2021, Raam [became a member of the governing coalition](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/04/world/middleeast/raam-palestinian-israel-government.html) — a watershed for a mainstream Arab party in Israeli politics. Mr. Abbas faced intense criticism for the decision, but he has continued to call for playing a direct role in decision-making, even if that means being saddled with blame for policies that Arab citizens find objectionable. “We are ready to pay the price,” he told The Times during the most recent election campaign.

Raam was founded in 1996 by a branch of the Islamic Movement in Israel, which works to strengthen Muslim identity and empower the country’s Arab minority.

In August, Mr. Abbas and Yoav Segalovitz, a veteran Zionist politician and former police commander, announced that [Mr. Segalovitz would run for the Knesset](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/31/world/middleeast/israel-raam-recruits-zionist.html) on Raam’s list. In teaming up, they offered themselves as an example of Jewish-Arab cooperation.

“There are people who are afraid of partnership,” Mr. Abbas said. “There are parties that are afraid of partnership. They are afraid of what people will say, afraid of what they will lose. Raam is not afraid of partnership. Raam advances it.”

items.title: How a Little-Known Company Dominated the Persian Gulf Oil Trade
items.summary: South Korea’s Sinokor controls about half the tanker transits through the Strait of Hormuz, benefiting from a big bet just before the war in Iran started.
items.full_text:
Title: How a Little-Known Company Dominated the Persian Gulf Oil Trade - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/business/sinokor-oil-tankers-strait-hormuz-shipping-iran.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:15:15 GMT

Markdown Content:
Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have [rebounded](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/business/oil-exports-strait-of-hormuz.html) in the past few months, as tankers have braved constant Iranian attacks to get their cargo out of the Persian Gulf.

The recovery rests largely on the efforts of an enigmatic South Korean shipping company.

That company, Sinokor, has accounted for about a half of the tanker transits through the strait since the beginning of September, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence, a maritime analysis firm.

“They’ve played a huge role in getting oil out of Hormuz, no doubt,” said Tomer Raanan, a senior maritime intelligence analyst at Lloyd’s List.

But concentrating so much oil in the hands of one tanker company could be adding to the cost of shipments out of the Middle East and across the world — rates that have already been pushed higher by the greater risk the war has forced on much of the global oil trade.

In an exceptionally well-timed bet, Sinokor, led by a father and son who are little known even in South Korea, began a buying spree in the two months before the United States and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February. It is now, by some counts, the largest operator of supertankers in the world.

While many tankers are tied up shuttling oil through the strait, creating shortages elsewhere, Sinokor’s growth has given it outsize power, said Kristoffer Barth Skeie, an equity analyst specializing in tanker companies for Arctic Securities.

“They have succeeded in cornering the market,” he said.

Sinokor owns 129 very large crude carriers — the industry name for tankers capable of carrying two million barrels of oil — up from 42 in December, according to BRS Shipbrokers.

Sinokor’s chairman, Chung Tae-soon, and his son, Chung Ga-hyun, have kept a low profile in South Korea. His father’s only public role seems to be as the head of the South Korean association that oversees Baduk, the board game also known as Go.

Founded in 1989, Sinokor operated the first container liner service between South Korea and China — a joint venture between South Korean and Chinese entities that started three years before the two nations established diplomatic ties. Chung Tae-soon eventually took full control of the company, according to South Korean media reports.

Employees of Sinokor declined to take calls from a reporter seeking comment from the company.

Sinokor’s dominance of Strait of Hormuz traffic was in part made possible by the U.S. military, which since May has run an extensive operation to shield vessels from Iranian drone and missile [attacks](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/business/hormuz-oil-tanker-attacks.html). The operation was aimed at neutralizing Iran’s threat to shipping and encouraging tanker operators to come back to the strait.

Many shipping companies have stayed away, but Sinokor and shipping companies controlled by the governments of the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have returned in earnest.

Many of the journeys that Sinokor is making through the strait are known as ship-to-ship transfers. They work like this: Tankers carry oil through the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman, and then transfer it to tankers that travel to the importing countries, mostly in Asia. Some Sinokor ships also sail directly to Asia, according to several analysts.

Despite the great efforts to get crude out, the price of oil remains far higher than before the war. That’s in part because demand for oil remains strong, and because of fears that the United States and Israel will again [attack targets in Iran](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/us-israel-renewed-iran-strikes.html), which might then target Persian Gulf energy facilities.

Even if hostilities cease, companies that own and operate tankers will continue to charge more to get oil out of the gulf, analysts say.

“It’s never going to be back to its prewar days, when shipping through the strait was cheap and easy and everybody did it,” said Rosemary Kelanic, a director at Defense Priorities, a research organization focused on foreign affairs.

The concentration of tankers in the hands of fewer players may have long-term implications for freight rates. Last year, the top three supertanker owners controlled 16 percent of the market, compared with 27 percent today, said John Cotzias, a co-founder of Xclusiv Shipbrokers, a Greek firm.

Veson Nautical, a maritime analysis firm, estimates that Sinokor spent $5.6 billion buying 70 tankers since the start of this year. Sinokor now owns 14 percent of the roughly 940 supertankers in operation. The next-largest owner and manager of very large crude carriers, China Merchants Group, controls about 5 percent of the market.

All along, shipping rates are rising. Tankers chartered for the 15-day run between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman have surged past $1 million per day, up from about $120,000 a day last year, Mr. Cotzias said.

“I’ve never seen these kind of rates,” he added.

Max Meizlish, a research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a research organization, said, “It seems very clear that this is part of Sinokor’s strategy — that they want to be a major player in setting freight rates.”

Meanwhile, mariners on ships in the Strait of Hormuz are working in dangerous conditions. More than 35 ships were attacked in October, more than in any other month of the war. Iran has struck at least seven Sinokor ships since July, including three in October, and 11 sailors were injured in an attack in July.

The Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a regulatory agency that Iran created in May in an attempt to establish authority over the strait, said last week that vessels belonging to Sinokor had committed the highest number of passage violations in recent months.

Manoj Yadav, the head of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, said he believed that shipowners had made maximizing profits a priority over ensuring the safety of sailors. Some shipping companies are paying higher wages to those willing to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, but that is not enough to cover the risks, he said.

items.title: ACLU’s Anthony Romero Says CEOs Are ‘Ducking the Hard Issues’
items.summary: Anthony Romero has led the American Civil Liberties Union since 2001. He worries that Americans have fewer rights now.
items.full_text:
Title: ACLU’s Anthony Romero Says CEOs Are ‘Ducking the Hard Issues’ - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/business/anthony-romero-aclu.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:34:33 GMT

Markdown Content:
Anthony Romero, the longtime leader of the American Civil Liberties Union, isn’t afraid to speak out against government policies that he sees as harmful. He wishes other chief executives would do the same.

Business leaders have appeared [reluctant to air their views](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/26/business/trump-disney-paramount-shareholder-capitalism.html) during President Trump’s second term. During that time, tariffs have disrupted supply chains and immigration raids have upended labor markets. [Law firms](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/16/us/politics/law-firms-deals-trump.html) and [media companies](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/18/business/media/trump-kimmel-cancel-culture-free-speech.html) cut deals and settled lawsuits that many experts said were winnable. Mr. Trump has regularly [cast doubt on the integrity of elections](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/09/us/politics/trump-elections-results-doubt-midterms.html) and pre-emptively challenged the [results of a midterm race in Alaska](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/us/politics/trumps-election-alaska.html) and [thousands of ballots in California](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/us/justice-dept-california-noncitizen-voters.html).

Mr. Romero, 61, who has run the organization for the past 25 years, recognizes that his role is not akin to that of a chief executive who answers to shareholders. But he believes that corporate executives also have a role to play in defending democratic institutions. He has taken notice of the tech billionaires who donated to the A.C.L.U. during Mr. Trump’s first term but have not written checks this time around.

During the 2016 presidential campaign and first few months of the first Trump administration, the A.C.L.U.’s revenue more than doubled from the previous fiscal year. It waned during the Biden years and jumped again in the lead-up to Mr. Trump’s return to the White House, but half as fast as before.

Mr. Romero, who directs some 2,100 employees and more than $550 million in contributions, says that the A.C.L.U. still must be judicious about the cases it pursues.

“This is not a church,” he said at his office with a view of the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor. “Prayer is not enough. You have to have a plan.”

_This interview has been edited and condensed._

**What do you want to see from corporate C.E.O.s during the Trump administration?**

I’ve been frustrated with the lack of engagement. Many of them are ducking the hard issues, whether it’s freedom of speech, the integrity of our voting systems, the mass deportation of hundreds of thousands of immigrants, the undercutting of the freedom of the press or the assault on rule of law and the courts.

They don’t have to agree with me on immigration or trans rights, but they should think that the functioning of our electoral system is critical, regardless of who you vote for.

**Do you think executives should speak out on that publicly?**

They need to tie it back to their business. For some businesses that rely upon immigrant labor, it’s a core issue.

Assaults on the rule of law in America have massive implications for business because if the judiciary’s independence is questioned or threatened by the administration, it hurts the prospects of business.

But I don’t want corporate C.E.O.s to try to do my job. Because when they tried to do it, they did it poorly.

**Are you talking about 2020?**

Yes, exactly. In the aftermath of the murder of George Floyd, you had so many who wanted to rush to make statements about the police. They weren’t really committed, as you can see now with their backtracking. No one wants halfhearted measures. If you don’t really believe it, don’t do it.

**What do executives tell you in private?**

They tell me it’s hard and I say, “I understand.”

If the president, for instance, pulls out all the stops and tries to subvert the outcome of this election, then that’s a moment when profiles in courage will be noted. The leadership of the private sector should stand up.

I understand the worry about the government targeting companies. They have a fiduciary responsibility to their shareholders.

What I find more perplexing is in their private lives. I can list — although I won’t, I don’t kiss and tell — six Silicon Valley billionaires who wrote large checks to the A.C.L.U. in Trump 1.0 and not one of them is engaged with us today.

Some have changed their mind, and they have every right. Some of them are making pragmatic decisions and some are just afraid.

The point of being powerful and sometimes wealthy is that it gives you independence to do what you want, to speak your mind. For the very wealthy and the very powerful to feel afraid and to hide, I think is very troubling.

**One criticism that the A.C.L.U. receives is that it acts as a wing of the Democratic Party. So is there anything that the Trump administration is doing that the A.C.L.U. would defend?**

I can applaud them for not doing things as aggressively as they might.

**Where does the A.C.L.U. stand on how A.I. might affect civil liberties?**

We are taking our time to study it. I want to be sure we get it right.

There have already been a number of suits that we’ve done that challenged the racial discrimination in algorithms. We’ve got to make sure the civil rights laws are applied in that context.

I’m especially concerned with the rights of immigrants. You have almost $240 billion appropriated for immigration enforcement. How could A.I. be used as a tool to help further identify, track, detain and deport immigrants?

And Republicans and Democrats alike are criticizing the ubiquitous nature of Flock cameras. All of this is leading us to think about the implications of A.I. in our work.

Image

![Image 1: Mr. Romero, sitting at a table with his chin resting on clasped hands, looks directly at the camera.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/01/multimedia/01biz-corneroffice-ACLU-ztlj/01biz-corneroffice-ACLU-ztlj-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

“Assaults on the rule of law in America have massive implications for business,” Mr. Romero said.Credit...Ahmed Gaber for The New York Times

**I’ve heard you say that Americans have fewer rights now than when you became executive director in 2001. How does that make you think about your legacy at the A.C.L.U.?**

We’re going through a hard time, and the institutions that constrain power seem to be either breaking or struggling.

There will not be a quick fix. The institutions that constrain government power have been so weakened or dismantled that it will take a generation to rebuild them. You can’t just go back and reassemble the same Justice Department you had before Donald Trump.

At the same time, there have been successes that continue. I never imagined that gay people like me would be able to marry their loved one.

**Do you worry about what will happen to the institution when the next person sits in your seat?**

This is not the Anthony Civil Liberties Union, it is the American Civil Liberties Union.

We can lose Silicon Valley donors and still have the rank-and-file folks who are writing an average gift of $112 a year. The power of the organization is rooted in the card-carrying members and because of that, I don’t worry about the leadership _._

**Tell me about your upbringing.**

The first nine years of life in the Bronx and in the Castle Hill housing project. Then, the second nine years in Passaic County, N.J.

There was so much love in my family that I never knew we were humble until years later.

**Were you the first in your family to go to college?**

I’m the first to finish high school. My father finished the fourth grade. My mother finished the 10th grade. They didn’t know anything about college.

**When you were growing up, your father, who worked in a Manhattan hotel, filed a legal grievance with his union when he was passed over for a job. How did that impact you?**

When we wanted to leave the Bronx, my father applied to be a banquet waiter at the hotel. He was turned down initially. They said his English wasn’t good enough. He filed the grievance, and he became the first Latino to be a banquet waiter.

It was that filing and that promotion that changed the trajectory of our entire family, where we could just live very differently and better.

**How much does your upbringing impact your work at the A.C.L.U.?**

I was a beneficiary of every government program and institution meant to level the playing field. For me, it worked. I got a scholarship, I got aid, I lived in public housing, I got student loans. I’m a proud affirmative action baby. You don’t go from where I started to Princeton, Stanford and where I am now without affirmative action ripping open the doors.

I earned my grades, my successes and my failures, but all of these programs give us an equal opportunity to compete. That is the animating force of my work at the A.C.L.U. — let every person fully actualize who they want to be.

**It’s time for the lightning round. Favorite Supreme Court justice?**

Sonia Sotomayor.

**Why?**

Her opinions, her dissents, her integrity. I’ve known her a very long time.

**What’s something you’ve learned from one of your youngest employees?**

Speak your truth. Don’t be afraid of it.

**In hindsight, what’s a decision you would have done differently?**

Early on, I would have consulted my board more regularly. I was coming in as a chief executive and sometimes made decisions without the benefit of other people’s thoughts.

**Do you think C.E.O.s should admit mistakes more often?**

The only mistake you shouldn’t admit is the one you haven’t yet recognized.

**What is your most contrarian take?**

Divisiveness is not necessarily bad. I’d rather t

items.title: As Political Ad Spending Skyrockets, Broadcast TV Remains King
items.summary: Even though marketers have increasingly shifted their dollars to other media, local stations are reaping a bonanza during these midterm elections. Nowhere is this is more evident than in Texas.
items.full_text:
Title: As Political Ad Spending Skyrockets, Broadcast TV Remains King - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/business/media/advertising-paxton-talarico-texas-television.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:34:36 GMT

Markdown Content:
The deluge of political advertising in this year’s midterm elections is shattering previous records.

Almost half of that money is going to a surprising place: your local TV channel.

Advertisers, following the changing viewing habits of Americans, have increasingly shifted their marketing dollars to social platforms, streaming channels and other digital media. Yet when it comes to federal and state races, politicians and PACs are brushing aside concerns that TV ads are costlier to produce and less efficient in targeting prospective voters — and are showering local stations with billions of dollars.

This election will show how much that calculus still holds in a transformed media environment.

“I think the Democrats and Republicans are both spending a disproportionate amount of their budgets on broadcast TV at this point,” said Danielle Butterfield, a Democratic strategist and the executive director of Priorities USA. “Because you can see so clearly what’s happening on the other side, there’s this muscle memory needing to chase and match.”

Political consultants and television executives argue that while broadcast TV may not be what it once was, those ads can reach a larger swath of the population more quickly than through other media. And that audience watching their nightly news programs, not to mention their favorite sitcoms, dramas and football games, is a devoted one.

“Local anchors and reporters are trusted, familiar voices,” said Gregg Siegel, senior vice president of national sales at Sinclair Broadcast Group, one of the country’s largest owners of local TV stations. “They don’t just cover the communities they serve. They live there, raise their families there and are part of the fabric of those communities. That connection creates a level of credibility that is difficult to replicate on other platforms.”

The amount of money being spent on political advertising this election cycle is staggering, helping to boost the bottom lines of the biggest local broadcasting companies like Sinclair, Nexstar Media Group, Gray Media, Tegna and the E.W. Scripps Company.

The research firm S&P Global projects broadcast television advertising this year to [be 15 percent higher](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/2026/04/broadcast-political-ad-revenue-set-to-exceed-4-billion-in-2026) than the last nonpresidential election year in 2022. And political ad revenue alone is expected to account for 16.3 percent of total broadcast revenue for the year, which would be a record for a nonpresidential election year.

During this election cycle, total political advertising is expected to reach $11.6 billion by Election Day, according to AdImpact; $5.6 billion (48 percent) is flowing to broadcast. That dollar figure is even higher than the one during the 2024 presidential race, when $5.3 billion was spent on broadcast advertising, still 48 percent of the total.

That growth is an outlier in the overall advertising market, where TV’s share continues to shrink as do the overall dollars. In 2024, for example, TV made up 15 percent of all ad spending in the United States, according to the research firm eMarketer. This year, projections envision that figure to be 10 percent.

Nowhere is the broadcast TV blitz more evident than in Texas, where more than half a billion dollars will be spent in the Senate runoff, primaries and general election campaigns.

Oscar Rodriguez, the president of the Texas Association of Broadcasters, said stations in all 20 media markets across the state were seeing ad buys, rather than just a few individual markets. “This is an election where clearly every single vote is going to matter,” he said.

In the tight Senate race between Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate, and James Talarico, his Democratic opponent, $220 million had been spent on broadcast ads through Oct. 28, more than half of the total spending, according to AdImpact. The Paxton campaign and its Republican allies account for most of the broadcast TV outlays, and much of that has been [supported by Elon Musk](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/politics/elon-musk-ken-paxton-texas-senate-race.html), the world’s richest man with deep business ties to Texas.

Nick Maddux, a senior adviser to Mr. Paxton, said that it was most efficient for the campaign to spend money on linear television because of federal rules that ensure candidates (and at least for now, [political parties and joint fund-raising committees](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/us/politics/supreme-court-ads-political.html)) get low-cost TV ad rates.

The campaign’s statewide ad onslaught in October resulted in some ad breaks airing three Paxtons spots for every one Talarico ad.

“You go big and fast,” Mr. Maddux said.

Luke Warford, a Democratic political consultant in Texas and chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party, said the Talarico campaign had focused more on building Mr. Talarico’s brand on social media. But the campaign and its Democratic allies have still spent heftily on broadcast TV, devoting 45 percent of their budgets to the medium through Oct. 28, according to AdImpact. (Republicans are at 60 percent.)

Advertising on television can be a blunt force approach to reaching prospective voters, particularly in House races where viewers are often bombarded with ads for candidates in districts not their own. Danilo Yanich, a University of Delaware professor who runs the school’s Local Television News Project, said that’s a trade-off campaigns and PACs will take. “They’ll tolerate those inefficiencies because they’re not sure which voters they will not reach if they try to do those directed kinds of advertising campaigns.”

“Local television viewers are very serious voters,” he added.

And the people who watch broadcast television are often those who vote.

“The kinds of people who tend to be very likely to vote in midterm elections tend to lean older,” Joshua Kalla, a professor of political science at Yale, said. “And those people still watch a whole bunch of broadcast TV.”

There’s another incentive driving this advertising strategy: money. Consultants and media buying firms typically take up to a 15 percent commission on their ad buys, which, given some of the multimillion dollar spends, can quickly add up.

Aaron Evans, a Republican campaign consultant, said that while broadcast had historically “been the beast that moves the numbers,” it was getting less effective every election cycle.

“The thing that is making that industry really outlast its effectiveness is the fact its been a cash cow for these consulting firms for decades,” he said.

Image

![Image 1: Elon Musk in a dark suit, white shirt and silver tie, sitting, with rows of people behind him.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/23/multimedia/TEXAS-ADS-1-03-wlzk/TEXAS-ADS-1-03-wlzk-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Much of the ad spending for Mr. Paxton is supported by Elon Musk, the world’s richest man with deep business ties to Texas.Credit...Demetrius Freeman for The New York Times

Some political operatives bemoan what they see as an outdated approach to advertising. During this year’s primaries, several candidates who were vastly outspent on TV ads still prevailed, including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed over his Democratic rival, Haley Stevens, in Michigan.

Ms. Butterfield, the Democratic strategist, pointed to internal research from Priorities USA that found that 83 percent of registered voters reported in using YouTube and 82 percent used streaming services in a single week in September, while just 61 percent said they watched linear TV. She said that ads on digital platforms, which were much cheaper than TV ads, could see a higher reach and have a more targeted impact.

“The biggest difference between a broadcast television strategy and a digital strategy is how much the campaign actually uses the internet to not just broadcast and shout at a voter, but understand where that voter is, what they care about,” she said.

Mr. Warford, the Democratic political consultant, said Tuesday’s vote would help answer a question about the broadcast television-heavy ad strategy in support of Mr. Paxton. “Is there an amount of money that can save an incredibly weak candidate in a tough environment at the end?”

items.title: Cyril Hilsum, Who Helped Invent Flat-Panel Displays in TVs and iPhones, Has Died at 101
items.summary: The man who helped develop the technology for liquid crystal displays — the screens in flat-panel televisions and laptops — has died at 101.
items.full_text:
Title: Cyril Hilsum, Who Helped Invent Flat-Panel Displays in TVs and iPhones, Has Died at 101 - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/technology/cyril-hilsum-dead.html

Published Time: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 10:01:18 GMT

Markdown Content:
In the beginning, televisions were barely smaller than Buicks. They weighed upward of 500 pounds. Finding a spot for them in the house was a challenge.

“Since we got our television set,” a TV World reader wrote to the magazine in 1953, “we’ve had to change the arrangement of furniture in our living room, and we just can’t keep the piano.”

In the 1960s, up to their antennas in complaints about these space- and power-hungry monstrosities, electronics executives and government regulators prodded scientists to find ways to shrink them. Defense officials joined in, hoping for smaller radar screens.

At the center of this herculean effort was Cyril Hilsum, an exuberant British physicist with voluminous, untamed white hair whose striking resemblance to Albert Einstein wasn’t limited to appearance.

“People say Einstein’s I.Q. was 155 or something, and I’d guess that Cyril’s was way higher than that,” J. Cliﬀ Jones, a physicist formerly affiliated with the University of Leeds in England, said in an interview. “I’m not saying Einstein wasn’t extremely important, but Cyril was that kind of man. He was that sharp.”

At the Royal Radar Establishment, a government research center, Dr. Hilsum led the team that developed crucial materials and technology for liquid crystal displays — the screens in flat-panel televisions, laptops and smartphones.

Image

Dr. Hilsum at the Services Electronics Research Laboratory, a military facility in Hertfordshire, in 1962.Credit...via Hilsum Family

Dr. Hilsum died on Sept. 23 at an assisted-living facility in London, his family said. He was 101, having survived into his 11th decade by avoiding fresh vegetables and subsisting largely on TV dinners, chocolate and red wine.

The son of street vendors in the gritty East End of London, Dr. Hilsum was an inventing machine. He developed semiconductors that are used in remote controls, automatic doors, burglar alarms and bar-code scanners.

His work with radar technology led to the development of Claribel, a device used to detect the location of snipers in Northern Ireland, and he was also instrumental in developing radar speed detectors, which occasionally caught him exceeding the posted limits on highways.

“He didn’t have a lot of time for theoretical physics or theoretical physicists,” his daughter Lindsey Hilsum, an author and [foreign correspondent](https://www.channel4.com/news/by/lindsey-hilsum) for TV news, said at his memorial service. “He was a materials scientist and an engineer. It was all about applications.”

In the late 1960s, Dr. Hilsum was working on radar for the British government when his boss inquired whether there might be something he could do about the size of electronic screens.

Radar displays and early TVs were behemoths because they used bulky cathode ray tubes (or CRTs) to beam images into thick, heavy sheets of glass. Wood cabinets housed and protected the finicky gear, turning these contraptions into unwieldy pieces of furniture.

“The CRT,” Dr. Hilsum [wrote](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsta/article/368/1914/1027/114001/Flat-panel-electronic-displays-a-triumph-of) in a 2010 article for Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, “was becoming more and more exposed as a dinosaur.”

At first, he wasn’t optimistic that anything could be done, but there was a new idea emerging — using liquid crystals to form images on a screen — that intrigued him.

For one thing, the crystals would use a lower voltage than CRTs. But more important, they could fit into a thin film between two slim sheets of glass. Goodbye, tubes.

The problem: Liquid crystals were stable only at high temperatures, and they dissolved quickly. No one would want to buy a new TV every few weeks.

Dr. Hilsum assembled a team of scientists to tackle the issue. The story of what they did could fill a five-part television series, but if reduced to the length of a caption in TV Guide, it would read something like this: “Scientists create a new family of stable liquid crystals known as cyanobiphenyls.”

The implications were immense.

“The world had been trying hard to find a stable material, and suddenly we had it,” Dr. Hilsum said in a 2020 [interview](https://archivesit.org.uk/interviews/cyril-hilsum-cbe/) with the journal Archives of Information Technology.

Digital watches arrived first, followed by pocket calculators, laptops, flat-screen televisions and, eventually, smartphones.

Dr. Hilsum became known as “the father of liquid crystals,” according to The Times of London. In 1976, [Queen Elizabeth II](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/08/world/europe/queen-elizabeth-dead.html) visited his lab and was photographed laughing as he tried to explain the technology to her.

“There were a lot of people involved in this technology, but Cyril pushed it in the direction it needed to go, and changed the world,” Dr. Jones said. “You can now fit a massive HDTV in your living room. That all comes down to this key invention.”

Image

In 1976, Queen Elizabeth II visited Dr. Hilsum’s lab and was photographed laughing as Dr. Hilsum, center, tried to explain the technology behind liquid crystal displays to her and Prince Philip, left.Credit...via Hilsum Family

The second of three boys, Mr. Hilsum was born in London on May 17, 1925, to Benjamin and Ada (Goldstein) Hilsum, who sold flat hats, chocolate and chamois leathers at stalls in Petticoat Lane and on Portobello Road.

His childhood was spartan and hardscrabble. “There was an outside loo, I can remember that,” he said in a 2002 oral history for the British Library. “We all slept, the three boys, in what seemed an enormous bed.”

Clothes were handed down or inherited from cousins. There were no presents on holidays.

“We played in the street,” he said. “We had fights. In general, I suppose it was like most families.”

But Cyril wasn’t like most other children. At 3, he was already reading. For fun, he took his toys apart.

“I wouldn’t interfere with electricity or anything like that,” he said. “But I would take toys to pieces, whether they were mine or other people’s.”

After high school, he won a scholarship to attend University College London. “I don’t know that Mum ever took it in,” he said. “Dad was thrilled. I mean, essentially it’s what he would have wanted to do.”

He studied math and physics, graduating in 1945, and received his doctorate in physics from the University of London in 1959.

Asked in the oral history what makes a good physicist, Dr. Hilsum replied: “Curiosity, curiosity. Always, you have the kind of mind that you want to know the answer to questions. You see something and you think, ‘How does that work?’ or ‘What would make that work better?’”

He said he had no interest in theoretical physics — not even the [Higgs boson](https://www.nytimes.com/topic/subject/higgs-boson) particle. “It would leave me completely flat,” he said. “I want things to work.”

He married Betty Cooper, his co-star in a college production of “Pygmalion,” in 1947, and frequently bought her gadgets as gifts, which he proceeded to take apart. She died in 1987. After their daughter Karen Burt, an engineer, died in 1997, Dr. Hilsum established a [scholarship](https://www.wes.org.uk/karen-burt-memorial-award) in her name with the Women’s Engineering Society.

In addition to his daughter Lindsey, Dr. Hilsum is survived by his partner, Anne Dell; a grandson; and his brother Charles, who is 103.

Image

Dr. Hilsum in 2020. Even at an advanced age, he continued inventing; he received his final patent when he was 97.Credit...via Hilsum Family

Dr. Hilsum held more than 70 patents. He received his last when he was 97. The [paperwork](https://patents.google.com/patent/EP4680792A1/en?q=G01L5%2f101&inventor=Cyril+Hilsum&sort=new) describes the invention as an “apparatus for, or methods of, measuring force, work, mechanical power or torque, specially adapted for specific purposes for measuring tension in flexible members, e.g. ropes, cables, wires, threads, belts or bands using electrical means using sensors inserted into the flexible member.”

In plain English, it’s an ink with sensors that can conduct electricity. One possible use is in hospital beds, to track the movement of patients and prevent bedsores. Dr. Hilsum developed the idea in his kitchen, where he set up lab equipment and worked in a white coat.

“You should always be concerned,” he once said, “with what you are doing that helps the community.”

items.title: How Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack Went Down
items.summary: A war room. A global conference call. A founder who live-posted about the largest crypto heist in history. Inside a frantic 24 hours at the world’s biggest crypto exchange.
